newsitem.title: USA: Amgen rejects link of Leptin to diabetes.
newsitem.headline: Amgen rejects link of Leptin to diabetes.

text.p: Amgen Inc Friday rejected a study that suggested leptin, a protein believed to cause weight loss, could cause diabetes. It said the test was conducted on cells in a petri dish and had no bearing on living animals.

"You can't extrapolate from a plastic dish to humans," said Amgen spokesman David Kaye. He said the company had tested the fat gene on rodents and animals and never found it to cause diabetes. In diabetic mice who were given leptin, in fact, their diabetes was normalized, he said.
A study published in the journal Science found that high levels of leptin disrupt some activities of insulin, the hormone that controls blood sugar levels.
But Kaye said Amgen, which is in the midst of its own study into the safety of leptin, "has not seen anything that would cause us to stop or change that trial one iota."
Salomon Bros biotechnology analyst Meirav Chovav also rejected suggestions that the Science study was a blow to Amgen's ongoing research into the potentially lucrative fat gene.
"There's a 99 percent chance it's totally irrelevant," she said of the Science study. "If it's not 99 percent, its 99.5 percent."
"You can pour iced tea on tissue culture cells and the cells will die. The analogy to what it will do (in a living animal) is ridiculous," Chovav added.
The findings published in Science were based on research done in tissue culture liver cells, or cells that are grown outside of the body.
The gene that produces leptin was discovered two years ago at Rockefeller University and has been shown to cause weight loss in mice. Amgen last year paid $20 million for rights to the gene.
